notes:
Research notes on IM8 (David Beckham-backed supplement brand from Prenetics). Question assumed to mean the Daily Ultimate Essentials powder. Searched Oct 12, 2026.

**What it is**
- The maker describes it as a third-party tested all-in-one supplement with 90 ingredients that replaces 16 capsules in a drink.
- A newer "Pro" version exists. It raised MSM to 1,500 mg, B12 to 200 mcg and K2 to 100 mcg, and added 30 mg of saffron extract. (getsupplementreviews.com, about 74 days old.)

**Positive findings**
- Trustpilot's summary (about 1,780 reviews) says reviewers overwhelmingly had a great experience. Praise centers on convenience and energy. Some customers said the powder can be grainy or hard to mix.
- Trustpilot also carries individual one-star reviews. One says the taste is so awful they can't get it down. Taste opinions are split.
- Several reviewers praise the taste, calling it berry-flavored, not grassy. These include running.reviews (a tester who was gifted the product) and trailandkale.com.
- The running.reviews tester reported less bloating and better digestion. They said it is expensive but worth it if it replaces 4 or 5 other supplements.
- Quality control looks solid. Both formulas are third-party tested and NSF Certified for Sport, with certificates published publicly.
- The company's own site claims 95% of participants felt more energy and 85% felt less bloated. This is the company's own marketing. The launch announcement said the 12-week trial was still ongoing.

**Critical findings**
- Innerbody rated it 3.8 overall, with effectiveness 7.5/10 (about 211 days old). It said Essentials could replace a multivitamin, probiotics and certain workout supplements, but otherwise its ingredient doses fall short of effective ranges. It also flagged key ingredient amounts hidden in proprietary blends and several underdosed ingredients.
- getsupplementreviews.com agrees that some blends are underdosed. The adaptogen and mushroom complex totals only 200 mg.
- Dietitian Abby Langer (about 88 days old) was harshly critical. She wrote that IM8 is clever marketing wrapped around science that is far weaker than consumers are led to believe. She also argued that having 90+ ingredients doesn't mean more benefit.
- Live it Up's dietitian (a competing brand, about 57 days old) called it one of the most expensive all-in-one supplements on the market, with extreme quantities of added vitamins and minerals.
- getsupplementreviews.com noted doubling up on vitamin A, zinc or niacin creates real upper limit concerns. It also noted reishi and grape seed can interact with blood thinners and blood pressure medication.

**Price**
- Prices vary by source. About $112 for a one-time 30-serving box and about $89 a month on subscription, per getsupplementreviews.com and Live it Up. An older review (trailandkale.com, about 33 days old) listed $79 on subscription and $99 one-time.
- Taking both IM8 formulas climbs past $196 monthly.

**Overall**
- Sources agree it is well made, tested and tastes decent for most people.
- They disagree on whether it delivers enough to justify the price. Enthusiastic reviews are mostly personal experiences, and some may be gifted or affiliate-linked. The critical reviews focus on doses, evidence and cost.
- I found no independent clinical evidence for its benefit claims.
